tasks.title: Read the four TCP/IP layers and map each one to something you already touched in Month 1.
Run ip addr on your VM and identify your IP address, your interface name and your MAC address.
Ping 127.0.0.1 and then ping your own IP. Work out why both succeed and what is different.
Find your VM private IP and your real public IP. Write down why they are not the same.
Learn the modern ip command and note which old ifconfig command each part replaces.
Start a networking section in your notes file for every command and term you meet this month.
Convert ten decimal octets to binary and back by hand until it stops being slow.
Break four IP addresses into their four octets and write each one in binary.
Read what the old address classes A, B and C were and why they were replaced.
Memorise the three private ranges: 10.x, 172.16 to 172.31, and 192.168.x.
Find out what 0.0.0.0, 127.0.0.1 and 255.255.255.255 each mean.
Look at one IPv6 address and learn only its shape. Do not study it further this month.
Learn what a subnet mask does and why 255.255.255.0 is the same as slash 24.
Write out a CIDR table from slash 24 to slash 30 with host counts, from memory.
For five given addresses, work out the network address and the broadcast address by hand.
Calculate usable host counts and explain why you subtract two.
Install ipcalc and use it to check every answer you worked out by hand.
Do twenty subnetting questions on paper. Time yourself. Record your score in your notes.
Split a slash 24 network into four equal subnets and list the range of each one.
Read what variable length subnet masking is and why real networks use unequal subnets.
Plan an address scheme for a fake company with three subnets: web, app and database.
Given two IPs and a mask, decide whether they can talk directly without a router.
Break it: set a wrong subnet mask on your VM, watch connectivity fail, then fix it.
Do twenty more subnetting questions and beat yesterday's time.
View your ARP table with ip neigh and explain what each entry is for.
Write down in your own words why a machine needs both a MAC address and an IP address.
Learn the difference between what a switch does and what a router does.
Clear your ARP cache, ping a device, then watch the entry reappear.
Read what a broadcast domain is and where it ends.
Print your routing table with ip route and explain every line in it.
Identify your default gateway and explain what happens to traffic with no matching route.
Add a static route manually, confirm it appears, then delete it again.
Run traceroute to a public site and count the hops between you and it.
Break it: remove your default route, watch the internet vanish, then restore it.
Read what IP forwarding is and check whether it is enabled on your VM.
Learn the four DHCP steps and what the client and server each send.
Find your current DHCP lease details on the VM and note when it expires.
Release and renew your DHCP lease and watch the address get reassigned.
Set a static IP on your VM with netplan and confirm it survives a reboot.
Break it: set a static IP that clashes with another device and observe what happens.
Learn the path a lookup takes: cache, resolver, root, TLD, then authoritative server.
Use dig on three domains and read the answer section properly.
Learn what A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT and NS records each do.
Run dig with plus trace on one domain and follow the whole path from root to answer.
Look at how your VM decides which DNS server to use and change it to 1.1.1.1.
Find the TTL on a record and explain why DNS changes are not instant.
Add an entry to /etc/hosts, point a fake name at your VM, and prove it works.
Work out whether /etc/hosts or DNS wins when both have an answer.
Compare the output of dig, host and nslookup on the same domain.
Break it: point your resolver at a dead DNS server, then diagnose the failure from symptoms alone.
Do a reverse lookup on an IP address and find out what PTR records are for.
Read how DNS caching works at the resolver and at the operating system.
Learn what a port is and why one IP address can run many services at once.
Memorise the common ports: 22, 25, 53, 80, 443, 3306 and 5432.
List every listening socket on your VM with ss and identify which process owns each.
Look at /etc/services and find three protocols you have never heard of.
Learn the difference between a service bound to 127.0.0.1 and one bound to 0.0.0.0.
Break it: start two services on the same port and read the error you get.
Write down three differences between TCP and UDP and one real use of each.
Learn the three way handshake and what SYN, SYN ACK and ACK mean.
Run ss and identify connections in ESTABLISHED, LISTEN and TIME WAIT states.
Use netcat to open a listener on one terminal and connect to it from another.
Send a file between two machines using netcat only.
Read how a TCP connection closes and what FIN does.
Use ping with a count and a size, and read what the round trip times tell you.
Install mtr and compare its live output to a plain traceroute.
Test whether a remote port is open using nc with the z flag.
Install nmap and scan only your own VM to see which ports are open.
Write a checklist for diagnosing a network fault, working from your machine outwards.
Use your own checklist to diagnose a fault a friend creates on your VM.
Capture traffic on your interface with tcpdump and stop it before the screen floods.
Filter a capture down to one host and one port.
Capture a real TCP handshake and identify the SYN, SYN ACK and ACK packets yourself.
Capture a DNS query and its response, then match them to what dig showed you.
Save a capture to a pcap file so you can open it later.
Capture an HTTP request and see the plain text. Understand why this matters.
Learn the parts of an HTTP request and an HTTP response.
Learn what GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE and HEAD are for.
Memorise what the 2xx, 3xx, 4xx and 5xx families mean, plus 200, 301, 404 and 502.
Use curl with -v on a real site and read every header in both directions.
Send a POST request with curl including a JSON body and a custom header.
Find three response headers on a real site and look up what each one does.
Compare your earlier plain text HTTP capture with an HTTPS one and see the difference.
Learn what a certificate chain is and what a certificate authority actually vouches for.
Use openssl to inspect a live site certificate and read its expiry date and issuer.
Generate a self signed certificate for your own VM.
Load your self signed site, read the browser warning, and explain why it appears.
Break it: use an expired or wrong name certificate and watch the exact error it produces.
Install Wireshark on your host machine and open the pcap file you saved on day 39.
Learn three display filters: by IP, by port and by protocol.
Use follow TCP stream on an HTTP conversation and read the whole exchange.
Write down when you would reach for tcpdump and when for Wireshark.
Compare an HTTP stream and an HTTPS stream side by side in Wireshark.
Configure nginx to serve a simple static site from a folder you choose.
Learn the structure of an nginx config: http, server and location blocks.
Set up two server names on one nginx instance and test both with the hosts file.
Find the nginx access log and error log and generate entries in both.
Learn why nginx -t before a reload saves you from taking a site down.
Break it: introduce a config error, watch the reload refuse, then read the message and fix it.

days.title: Second Machine And Machine To Machine Traffic

tasks.title: Create a second VM on the same host network and confirm the two can ping each other.
Give both machines hostnames and make them reachable by name using the hosts file.
Run a simple web app on VM two listening on port 8080 and reach it from VM one with curl.
Compare the listening sockets on both machines and note what each one exposes.
Capture the traffic between the two VMs with tcpdump and confirm what you expect to see.
Enable ufw and set a default policy of deny incoming and allow outgoing.
Allow SSH and HTTP, then confirm both still work while other ports are blocked.
Read ufw status verbose and explain every rule listed.
Prove a blocked port is really blocked by testing it from the second VM.
Break it: block SSH, lose your connection, then recover through the VM console.
Read why firewall rule order matters and what happens on first match.
List the current iptables rules and find the ones ufw created for you.
Learn what the INPUT, OUTPUT and FORWARD chains do.
Add one iptables rule by hand, test it, then remove it.
Learn what NAT does and why many devices can share one public IP.
Set up a port forward so traffic hitting VM one reaches a service on VM two.
Read that nftables is replacing iptables on modern systems.
Create a local port forward and reach a service on VM two through VM one.
Learn what a remote port forward does and when you would need one.
Use a jump host to reach a machine you cannot connect to directly.
Tunnel a database port over SSH and connect to it as if it were local.
Write down why tunnelling is safer than opening a port to the whole internet.
Configure nginx on VM one to proxy requests to the app on VM two.
Pass the real client IP through the proxy using the forwarded headers.
Close port 8080 on VM two so the app is only reachable through the proxy.
Trace one single request through the proxy log and then the app log.
Break it: stop the backend app and study the 502 error nginx returns.
Write down four jobs a reverse proxy does in a real system.
Define an upstream block in nginx with two backend targets.
Send repeated requests and prove they alternate between the two backends.
Stop one backend and watch traffic continue through the healthy one.
Terminate TLS at nginx so the outside is HTTPS and the inside stays HTTP.
Redirect all HTTP traffic to HTTPS and confirm it with curl.
Read what session stickiness is and why it complicates load balancing.

days.title: Capstone: Build It, Break It, Prove It

tasks.title: Build the full stack: app on VM two, nginx reverse proxy on VM one, firewall locked down.
Serve the site over HTTPS with your certificate and no plain HTTP reachable.
Have a friend break one thing at any layer without telling you what it was.
Diagnose the fault using your day 38 checklist, tcpdump and the logs. No guessing.
Write the whole build up as a README with a diagram of the traffic path.
Push the configs and the README to your GitHub repo from Month 1.
Review your networking notes and mark every command you still cannot recall unaided.

questions.prompt: What does the slash 24 in 192.168.1.0/24 tell you?
options: The first 24 bits are the network part
questions.explanation: CIDR notation counts how many leading bits belong to the network portion of the address.

questions.prompt: Which subnet mask matches slash 24?
questions.explanation: Twenty four network bits produce three full octets of 255 followed by a zero.

questions.prompt: How many usable host addresses are in a slash 24 network?
questions.explanation: Of the 256 addresses, one is the network address and one is the broadcast address.

questions.prompt: Why do you subtract two when counting usable hosts?
options: For the router and the switch
For the network address and the broadcast address
questions.explanation: The lowest address identifies the network and the highest is reserved for broadcast.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a private address range?
questions.explanation: 192.168.0.0/16 is one of the three reserved private ranges, along with 10.x and 172.16 to 172.31.

questions.prompt: What is 127.0.0.1 used for?
questions.explanation: The loopback address always points back at the local machine.

questions.prompt: Which command shows your IP address on a modern Linux system?
questions.explanation: The ip command replaced the older ifconfig tool on current distributions.

questions.prompt: How many usable hosts does a slash 30 network give you?
questions.explanation: A slash 30 has four addresses in total, and two of them are reserved.

questions.prompt: What is the broadcast address of 192.168.10.0/24?
questions.explanation: The broadcast address is the highest address in the range, with all host bits set to one.

questions.prompt: If you split a slash 24 into four equal subnets, what mask do you get?
questions.explanation: Borrowing two host bits produces four subnets and gives a slash 26.

questions.prompt: What is a MAC address used for?
options: Identifying a device on the local network segment
questions.explanation: MAC addresses work at the local link level, while IP addresses route across networks.

questions.prompt: Two devices with the same subnet mask but different network portions can talk directly without a router.
questions.explanation: If their network portions differ they are on different networks, so traffic has to go through a router.

questions.prompt: A private IP address can be reached directly from the public internet.
questions.explanation: Private ranges are not routable on the internet, which is why NAT exists.

questions.prompt: Setting the wrong subnet mask can break connectivity even when the IP address itself is correct.
questions.explanation: The mask decides which destinations are treated as local, so a wrong mask sends traffic the wrong way.

questions.prompt: Every device needs both an IP address and a MAC address to communicate on a normal network.
questions.explanation: The IP address gets traffic across networks and the MAC address delivers it on the final segment.

questions.prompt: What does ARP do?
options: Maps an IP address to a MAC address
questions.explanation: ARP finds the hardware address that belongs to a known IP on the local segment.

questions.prompt: What is the main difference between a switch and a router?
options: A switch works inside one network, a router connects different networks
questions.explanation: Switches forward within a segment using MAC addresses, and routers move traffic between networks using IP.

questions.prompt: What happens to a packet with no matching route in the routing table?
options: It goes to the default gateway
It is returned to the sender
questions.explanation: The default route is the catch all destination for anything not matched by a more specific route.

questions.prompt: Which command prints the routing table?
questions.explanation: ip route shows the routes the kernel will use to reach different destinations.

questions.prompt: What does traceroute show you?
options: The path and the hops between you and a destination
questions.explanation: Traceroute reveals each router along the path, which helps you find where a problem starts.

questions.prompt: How many messages are in the standard DHCP exchange?
questions.explanation: Discover, offer, request and acknowledge make up the four step exchange.

questions.prompt: What is a DHCP lease?
options: A time limited assignment of an address
questions.explanation: Leases expire so addresses can be reclaimed and reused.

questions.prompt: In DNS, what does an A record hold?
questions.explanation: The A record maps a hostname to an IPv4 address.

questions.prompt: What does a CNAME record do?
options: Points a name at another name
Points a name at an IP
questions.explanation: A CNAME is an alias that redirects one hostname to another hostname.

questions.prompt: Which record type tells you where email for a domain should go?
questions.explanation: MX records identify the mail servers responsible for a domain.

questions.prompt: What does the TTL on a DNS record control?
options: How long the domain is registered
How long resolvers may cache the answer
How many hops the query can take
How long the server waits before timing out
questions.explanation: TTL is the cache lifetime, which is why DNS changes take time to appear everywhere.

questions.prompt: Which usually wins when a name exists in both /etc/hosts and DNS?
questions.explanation: On a default configuration the local hosts file is consulted before DNS.

questions.prompt: Clearing your ARP cache permanently stops the entries from coming back.
questions.explanation: Entries are rebuilt automatically the next time the machine needs to reach that address.

questions.prompt: A DNS change can appear instantly for one person and hours later for another.
questions.explanation: Caching at different resolvers means the old answer survives until its TTL expires.

questions.prompt: Removing your default route will usually break internet access while leaving local traffic working.
questions.explanation: Local destinations still match specific routes, but everything else has nowhere to go.

questions.prompt: Why can one IP address serve many different applications?
options: Each service listens on a different port
questions.explanation: Ports let a single address separate traffic between many listening services.

questions.prompt: Which port does HTTPS use by default?
questions.explanation: Port 443 is the standard for HTTPS, while 80 is plain HTTP.

questions.prompt: Which port does SSH use by default?
questions.explanation: SSH listens on port 22 unless it has been deliberately changed.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between binding to 127.0.0.1 and 0.0.0.0?
options: 127.0.0.1 is local only, 0.0.0.0 accepts connections on all interfaces
questions.explanation: Binding to loopback keeps a service private to the machine, while 0.0.0.0 exposes it to the network.

questions.prompt: What are the three steps of the TCP handshake?
questions.explanation: The client sends SYN, the server replies SYN ACK, and the client confirms with ACK.

questions.prompt: Which protocol does not guarantee delivery?
questions.explanation: UDP sends without acknowledgement, which makes it fast but unreliable.

questions.prompt: Which command lists listening sockets and the processes that own them?
questions.explanation: The ss command shows socket state and can display the owning process.

questions.prompt: What does an HTTP 404 status mean?
questions.explanation: 404 means the server understood the request but has nothing at that path.

questions.prompt: What does an HTTP 502 status usually indicate?
options: A proxy could not get a valid response from the backend
questions.explanation: A 502 means the gateway or proxy reached out to the backend and got nothing usable.

questions.prompt: What family do 3xx status codes belong to?
questions.explanation: Codes in the 300 range tell the client the resource is somewhere else.

questions.prompt: Which curl flag shows the full request and response headers?
questions.explanation: The -v flag turns on verbose mode and prints headers in both directions.

questions.prompt: What does tcpdump let you do that ping does not?
options: Test if a host is up
Inspect the actual packets on the wire
questions.explanation: tcpdump captures real traffic so you can see exactly what was sent and received.

questions.prompt: Traffic sent over plain HTTP can be read by anyone capturing packets on the path.
questions.explanation: Without TLS the request and response travel in readable text, which a capture will show in full.

questions.prompt: Two services can listen on the same port on the same interface at the same time.
questions.explanation: The second one fails to bind, which is why you get an address already in use error.

questions.prompt: A GET request is meant to retrieve data rather than change it.
questions.explanation: GET is defined as a safe method, so changes should use POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE instead.

questions.prompt: What does a certificate authority actually vouch for?
options: That a site is safe to use
That the certificate holder controls the named domain
That the site has no bugs
questions.explanation: A CA verifies control of the domain, not the quality or honesty of the site.

questions.prompt: Why does a browser warn about a self signed certificate?
options: No trusted authority vouches for it
questions.explanation: The browser has no chain of trust leading back to an authority it already trusts.

questions.prompt: Which tool inspects a live site certificate from the command line?
questions.explanation: openssl s_client connects and shows the presented certificate and its chain.

questions.prompt: What happens when a certificate expires?
options: The site loads with no change
Clients refuse or warn about the connection
questions.explanation: Expiry breaks trust, so clients warn or refuse to continue.

questions.prompt: In an nginx config, which block defines how a particular URL path is handled?
questions.explanation: The location block matches request paths and sets the rules for them.

questions.prompt: What does nginx -t do?
questions.explanation: Testing the config first prevents a reload from taking the site offline.

questions.prompt: Which nginx log records requests that were served?
questions.explanation: The access log lists served requests, while the error log records failures.

questions.prompt: What is a sensible default firewall policy for a server?
questions.explanation: Blocking inbound by default and opening only what you need is the standard safe posture.

questions.prompt: What is the danger of enabling a firewall over an SSH session?
options: You can block SSH and lock yourself out
questions.explanation: If SSH is not explicitly allowed, enabling the firewall cuts your own connection.

questions.prompt: Which iptables chain handles traffic arriving for the local machine?
questions.explanation: INPUT covers packets destined for the machine itself.

questions.prompt: What problem does NAT solve?
options: Many devices sharing one public IP address
questions.explanation: NAT translates private addresses to a shared public one so many devices can reach the internet.

questions.prompt: Which tool would you use to read a saved pcap file with a graphical interface?
questions.explanation: Wireshark opens capture files and makes filtering and stream following much easier.

questions.prompt: Firewall rules are evaluated in order and the first match usually decides the outcome.
questions.explanation: Because the first matching rule wins, putting a broad deny above a specific allow blocks the traffic.

questions.prompt: Terminating TLS at a reverse proxy means the connection behind the proxy can be plain HTTP.
questions.explanation: The proxy handles encryption with the client and can speak unencrypted to a backend on a trusted network.

questions.prompt: A self signed certificate encrypts traffic just as strongly as one from a public authority.
questions.explanation: The encryption is the same, and what is missing is the trust chain that stops impersonation.

questions.prompt: What does proxy_pass do in an nginx config?
options: Forwards the request to a backend server
questions.explanation: proxy_pass sends the request onward to the backend and returns its response to the client.

questions.prompt: Why close the backend port after putting a reverse proxy in front of it?
options: So the backend can only be reached through the proxy
questions.explanation: Closing the direct route forces all traffic through the proxy, where your rules and TLS live.

questions.prompt: You get a 502 from your proxy. What should you check first?
options: Whether the backend service is running
questions.explanation: A 502 means the proxy could not get a usable response, so the backend is the first suspect.

questions.prompt: What does an upstream block define in nginx?
options: A group of backend servers to send traffic to
questions.explanation: The upstream block names the backends that nginx can balance requests across.

questions.prompt: What is the default way nginx distributes requests across an upstream group?
questions.explanation: Round robin sends each new request to the next backend in the list.

questions.prompt: Why does a reverse proxy need to forward the original client IP?
options: Because otherwise the backend only sees the proxy address
questions.explanation: Without the forwarded header, every request in the backend logs looks like it came from the proxy.

questions.prompt: What does an SSH local port forward achieve?
options: It opens a port on the internet
It makes a remote service reachable on a local port through the tunnel
questions.explanation: The tunnel carries traffic from a local port to a service reachable from the SSH server.

questions.prompt: Why is tunnelling a database port over SSH safer than opening it publicly?
options: The port is never exposed to the internet
questions.explanation: Nothing is listening publicly, so attackers have no port to reach in the first place.

questions.prompt: What is a jump host used for?
options: Reaching a machine you cannot connect to directly
questions.explanation: You connect through an intermediate machine that does have access to the target.

questions.prompt: You can ping a server but cannot load its website. What is the most likely cause?
options: The service or the port is blocked or down
questions.explanation: Successful pings prove the network path works, so the problem sits at the service or firewall level.

questions.prompt: In a redirect from HTTP to HTTPS, which status code is normally used?
questions.explanation: A 301 tells the client the resource has permanently moved to the secure address.

questions.prompt: When diagnosing a fault, why start from your own machine and work outwards?
options: It narrows the problem down one layer at a time
questions.explanation: Checking locally first eliminates whole categories of cause before you look further away.

questions.prompt: If one backend in a load balanced pair stops, nginx can keep serving from the other one.
questions.explanation: Requests are directed to the remaining healthy backend, which is the main reason for running more than one.

questions.prompt: A reverse proxy sits in front of your servers, while a forward proxy sits in front of clients.
questions.explanation: The direction of the traffic it represents is what separates the two.

questions.prompt: Writing up how you diagnosed a fault is a waste of time once the fault is fixed.
questions.explanation: The write up is what turns a one off fix into a repeatable skill, and it is standard practice in operations work.
